_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 6 specification: one article, six gaps, SEVEN sentences A–G, one of them extra. Each removed sentence hooks backwards by reference (it, the conversation, such attitudes, also, for instance, these recordings) and forwards to the next sentence (today however, asked the old man, so she went, in the end, within a term though, several of them). The extra sentence (E) tempts gap 4, which is about Tomás's reaction, but 'agreed immediately' contradicts 'not enthusiastic at first' and leaves 'In the end… persuaded him' with nothing to resolve. Used by the Part 6 practice page.
title: The village that whistles
subtitle: In one mountain village, the old people still talk across the valleys without saying a word. A young teacher decided their language was too good to lose.
text: In the mountain village of Valdarre, the quickest way to send a message to the other side of the valley is not to phone. Mobile signal is patchy at best, and the paths between farms can take an hour to walk. For centuries, shepherds and farmers here have solved the problem with the silva, a whistled form of their language that can carry for more than two kilometres. {1} Today, however, fewer than thirty people can still use it, and the youngest of them is seventy-one.

Elena Brasca arrived in Valdarre six years ago to teach at the village school, which has just fourteen pupils. On her first morning she heard a high, bird-like call from the hillside opposite, followed by an answer from somewhere below the school. At first she assumed it was a pair of unusually talkative birds. {2} When she mentioned it to the old man who delivered the bread, he laughed and explained that two neighbours were arguing about a goat.

Elena soon discovered that the silva had never been written down, let alone taught in a classroom. Children grew up with smartphones, most of them left for the city as soon as they could, and many parents saw the whistling as something old-fashioned and slightly embarrassing. {3} So she went to see Tomás Ferrol, a retired shepherd of eighty-two who was widely considered the best whistler in the valley, and asked for his help.

Tomás was not enthusiastic at first. As a boy he had been punished for whistling in class, and the idea of doing it on purpose in a school struck him as ridiculous. {4} In the end, it was his granddaughter, one of Elena's pupils, who changed his mind by asking him to teach her how to whistle her own name.

Lessons began with one hour a week. Tomás whistled from one end of the school field while the children, standing at the other, tried to work out what he was saying. The early results were mixed. {5} Within a term, though, the class could understand simple messages, and two boys had learned to whistle 'Come home, dinner's ready' well enough to fool their mothers.

Word spread quickly. The silva is now taught to every pupil in the school, and a Saturday class for adults attracts people from the town further down the valley. The regional government has also paid for Tomás and the other remaining speakers to be recorded. {6} Several of them, according to Elena, had not been heard in the village for half a century.

For Tomás, though, the greatest reward is simpler. Every afternoon at four, his granddaughter whistles to him from the school gate, and he whistles back from his kitchen window. 'She asks what's for dinner,' he says. 'The answer is usually the same, but she likes to hear it.'
sentences: It was only when the conversation had gone on for a quarter of an hour that she began to have her doubts.
These recordings now include hundreds of words for plants, animals and types of weather that are no longer used in everyday speech.
He also doubted that children who spent their evenings on tablets would have the patience for something so difficult.
In the past, almost everyone in the village could understand it, from grandmothers to small children.
He agreed immediately, saying he had been waiting years for someone to ask.
Such attitudes, she realised, meant that the silva would disappear with its last speakers within a generation.
One girl, for instance, convinced she had been told to fetch a chair, came back proudly carrying a cheese.
why: 'It' is the silva; 'in the past, almost everyone' contrasts with 'Today, however, fewer than thirty people'.
'The conversation' is the call and the answer she took for birds; her 'doubts' lead her to ask the old man who delivered the bread.
'Such attitudes' are the parents' view that whistling was old-fashioned and embarrassing; the danger of the language disappearing explains 'So she went to see Tomás'.

'He also doubted' adds a second objection to the punishment he remembered; 'In the end' shows how those doubts were overcome. E is tempting, but 'agreed immediately' contradicts 'not enthusiastic at first'.
'For instance' gives an example of the 'mixed' early results; the chair-and-cheese mistake contrasts with 'Within a term, though'.
'These recordings' are the ones the regional government paid for; the old words are then picked up by 'Several of them… had not been heard'.
